A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and newly added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original memorization evaluations, noise and interpolation comparisons, modeling-factor ablations, symmetry experiments, and additional empirical analyses in its appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds data-scaling experiments, randomized-weight and training-length controls, statistical data-copying tests, and an ImageNet evaluation.

M1.justification: The four studied weight-generation methods and the noise, averaging, and fitted-Gaussian procedures remain unchanged. The additions evaluate these methods under further conditions and introduce an evaluation statistic, rather than modifying their generation algorithms.

E1.justification: Appendix I adds p-diff evaluation using ImageNet classification checkpoints, extending the earlier CIFAR-100 coverage. Existing classification, ShapeNet, Flowers, and intrinsic-dimension datasets remain; the coverage extension stays within the existing task families.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain Gaussian noise addition, checkpoint averaging, fitted-Gaussian sampling, and independently trained models where applicable. The new ImageNet experiment extends the existing interpolation comparison. Newly cited weight-generation methods are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols scale G.pt from 2.1M to 20.4M checkpoints and Hyper-Representations from 2896 to 24136. Other additions reinitialize individual or all MLP layers and compare independently initialized MLPs trained for 0, 200, 400, or full epochs. Appendix B adds holdout-based rank testing. These substantially expand the experimental design while retaining the original default experiments.

E4.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix F add substantial analyses of checkpoint scarcity, memorization of random weights, and dependence on MLP training progress. Appendix I tests whether greater downstream image diversity changes p-diff's behavior. The earlier model-size, regularization, and training-duration ablations remain in Appendix F.3.

E5.justification: v2 introduces non-parametric data-copying tests with standardized Mann-Whitney Z_U scores for original models and several ablations. Appendix B supplies HyperDiffusion sample counts and cautions against comparing scores across methods with different holdout sizes. The existing 20-seed from-scratch comparison and its accuracy variation are retained.

E6.justification: The added G.pt scaling experiment reports generated/training nearest-neighbor distances of 2.78/2.70, versus 2.25/3.64 under the original data size, with accuracy remaining approximately 94%. New statistical results show Z_U changing from -8.5 to 3.5 with G.pt scaling, while Hyper-Representations remains at -13.6. Randomized-weight and ImageNet findings are also added. Some Figure 6 scatter samples change, while v1 Table 1 is retained numerically as v2 Table 9.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds an extremal-score argument alongside the rank-test definitions: approximately -30.8 is the minimum attainable Z_U for n=606 and m=666, and the HyperDiffusion cases attain it. The existing symmetry discussion, IoU definition, and intrinsic-dimension estimator remain unchanged; no substantial theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central replication/interpolation and simple-baseline findings remain. However, the abstract, introduction, and conclusion now foreground limited data, overparameterization, and underused structural priors as potential explanations, and introduce data scaling as a successful mitigation in G.pt. This materially expands the central contributions beyond v1's emphasis on unsuccessful mitigation.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations involving dataset size and capacity, qualifies scaling benefits through Hyper-Representations' failure, and distinguishes downstream diversity from checkpoint diversity. Appendix H explicitly identifies architectural and training confounds in the image-versus-weight comparison. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation that unexamined methods may behave differently is removed.

D1.justification: v2 discloses more exact checkpoint/run counts, G.pt's 200 checkpoints per run, and HyperDiffusion's occupancy-field and mesh-extraction details. New experiments specify Kaiming Uniform initialization and an MLP stopping rule of 50 epochs without improvement. The existing project/code access information and CIFAR-100 training recipe remain.

R1.justification: v2 expands citations to recent weight-generation successors, data-copying detection, network expressivity, and policy-archive compression, while updating introductory image/video examples. It more explicitly challenges prior novelty claims, but retains its overall positioning as an empirical examination of weight-generation generalization.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially revised, the generic generative-model background subsection is removed, and Section 4 is reorganized around explanations of memorization. Earlier modeling-factor discussion moves to Appendix F.3, new appendices are integrated, and the standalone Limitations and Broader Impacts sections disappear. Headings and citation style change throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adds scaling/random-initialization histograms, statistical and ablation tables, and ImageNet heatmap and trade-off figures. It relocates the original main ablation table to the appendix and redraws existing scatter/t-SNE displays, including axis and marker changes. Title, heading, and page styling are revised throughout.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's unsuccessful mitigation tests, v2 establishes contrasting data-scaling outcomes, tests memorization of random weights, and adds holdout-based statistical and ImageNet checks. These substantially strengthen the evidence about when memorization occurs and what may alleviate it. The explicit confounds in Appendix H also improve interpretation. Although removing the untested-methods limitation weakens scope qualification, the added controls and more nuanced explanations provide a substantial net improvement.
